title: Beamer Classic — Computer Modern Theorem Lecture
description: A LaTeX-faithful lecture slide built around the Computer Modern typeface: definition box at top framed by a thin rule, italic theorem statement in body, and parenthesized-integer proof steps below. Structurally and typographically continuous with a compiled Beamer PDF.
philosophy: This template exists to honor the visual contract between mathematical writing and mathematical teaching — the idea that a slide should feel like a page from the same document as the problem set. It refuses decorative color, novelty display faces, and any layout element that doesn't map directly onto the logical structure of a formal argument. It is built for instructors who want the medium to vanish so the mathematics can speak. The room it serves is a lecture hall where students in the back row need to parse subscripts and overlines without visual noise competing for attention.
goodFor: Graduate-level math, physics, and CS lecture courses
Dense linear algebra or real analysis content requiring LaTeX notation fidelity
avoidFor: Marketing, brand, or investor pitch decks
Visual-driven photo essays or mood boards
General audiences with no exposure to formal mathematical notation
author: harness

examples.promptCore: The slide should feel indistinguishable from the title frame of a compiled LaTeX Beamer document — spare, authoritative, and utterly without decoration. Compositional rhythm is strictly vertical and centered, with hierarchy established through size contrast and rule lines alone, never through color fields or ornament. The mood is the quiet dignity of a chalkboard lecture: the medium effaces itself so that the course name and theorem topic carry full weight. Avoid any element — drop shadow, gradient, icon, or background texture — that would not appear in a default Beamer theme.

examples.layoutNotes: 12-column grid with content anchored in cols 3–10, vertically centered as a single stacked block occupying roughly the middle 50% of slide height. A full-width thin rule (hairline, 0.4pt equivalent) separates the course/lecture identifier line above from the main title below; a second rule of identical weight separates the title block from the instructor–institution–date cluster beneath. No header band, no footer bar — page number suppressed on title frame per Beamer convention. All elements flush to the same invisible center spine; outer columns serve only as breathing margin.

examples.promptCore: The slide feels like a page from a compiled Beamer PDF — austere, structurally legible, and typographically self-effacing. Compositional rhythm is strictly vertical: definition box, theorem body, and numbered proof steps each occupy their own register without decoration or bleed between layers. The mood is a chalkboard lecture made permanent — dense but never cluttered, formal without coldness, the structure doing all the visual work. Avoid rounded corners, gradient fills, icon decoration, or asymmetric tension; every element should feel placed by a typesetting algorithm, not a designer's hand.

examples.layoutNotes: The slide uses a tight single-column layout with roughly 8% outer margins on all sides, content spanning the full usable width. A definition or theorem block sits at the top, enclosed in a thin hairline rule box that bleeds edge-to-edge within the content column. Below it, an italic theorem statement fills the mid-body, followed by a parenthesized-integer hanging-indent proof-step list in the lower body. Slide number is anchored bottom-right flush with the margin; hierarchy is established through rule lines, indentation, and weight-plus-style contrast alone — no decorative dividers or color banding.
